hook.text: Press on a sealed fluid and the pressure spreads equally in every direction. Pascal discovered this in 1653.

buildup.text: Pressure applied at one point transmits undiminished to every point in the fluid and to the container walls.

discovery.text: A small piston pressing hard on fluid creates the same pressure at a large piston. Force multiplies by area ratio.

twist.text: You gain force but lose distance. Push the small piston ten centimeters and the large one moves one centimeter.

climax.text: Every hydraulic jack, car brake, and excavator arm runs on Pascal's principle. One idea, endless machines.

punchline.text: Pressure doesn't play favorites. It pushes on everything equally.

quiz.question: What does Pascal's principle state about pressure in a confined fluid?
options: Pressure decreases with distance from the point of application
Pressure transmits equally and undiminished in all directions
Pressure only acts downward due to gravity

hook.text: Hydraulic fluid isn't just oil. It transmits force, lubricates parts, prevents rust, and carries heat away.

buildup.text: The fluid must resist compression. Liquids are nearly incompressible — push one end and the other moves instantly.

discovery.text: Viscosity matters. Too thick and the fluid won't flow through small passages. Too thin and it leaks past seals.

twist.text: Water is a terrible hydraulic fluid. It boils at low temperatures, corrodes metal, and freezes in winter.

climax.text: Modern hydraulic oils work from minus 40 to 100 degrees Celsius. Additives protect against wear and oxidation.

punchline.text: The fluid does four jobs at once. Choose the wrong one and everything fails.

quiz.question: Why is water a poor choice as hydraulic fluid?
options: It is too viscous to flow through hydraulic passages quickly
It boils at low temperatures, corrodes metal, and freezes in cold weather
It compresses too easily under pressure to transmit force

hook.text: Push a syringe full of water — the plunger barely moves. Fill it with air and the plunger sinks easily.

buildup.text: Liquids resist compression. Their molecules are already tightly packed with almost no room to squeeze closer.

discovery.text: Gases compress easily. Their molecules have wide gaps. Push them together and they spring right back.

twist.text: Hydraulics use incompressible liquid for precise, rigid control. Pneumatics use compressible air for cushioned, springy motion.

climax.text: Air bubbles in hydraulic oil are dangerous. The system becomes spongy and unpredictable. Bleed the air out.

punchline.text: Liquid for precision. Gas for cushion. Know which you need.

quiz.question: Why are air bubbles dangerous in hydraulic systems?
options: They chemically react with the oil and cause corrosion
They make the system spongy and unpredictable because air compresses
They increase the fluid temperature beyond safe operating limits

topics.title: Flow Rate and Velocity: Moving the Fluid

hook.text: A hydraulic pump moves fluid at a set flow rate. More flow means faster cylinder speed, not more force.

buildup.text: Flow rate is volume per time — liters per minute. It determines how fast actuators move, not how hard they push.

discovery.text: Force comes from pressure. Speed comes from flow. A system with high pressure but low flow lifts heavy loads slowly.

twist.text: Narrow pipes increase fluid velocity but add friction losses. Wider pipes reduce friction but cost more.

climax.text: Engineers size pumps for flow and relief valves for pressure. Getting either wrong wastes energy or breaks things.

punchline.text: Pressure is strength. Flow is speed. They're independent.

quiz.question: What determines the speed of a hydraulic cylinder?
options: The system pressure set by the relief valve
The flow rate of fluid delivered by the pump
The diameter of the hydraulic hoses in the system

hook.text: Hydraulic power equals pressure times flow rate. Double either one and you double the power delivered.

buildup.text: A pump converts mechanical energy into fluid power. The motor or engine driving the pump sets the input.

discovery.text: Typical hydraulic systems run at 150 to 250 bar. Pressure that high packs enormous power into small cylinders.

twist.text: Efficiency is never 100%. Friction in valves and hoses converts some power to heat. The oil warms up.

climax.text: A compact hydraulic system delivers more power per kilogram than almost any other technology. That's why planes use it.

punchline.text: Pressure times flow equals power. Small pipes, huge force.

quiz.question: Why do aircraft prefer hydraulic systems for flight controls?
options: Hydraulic fluid weighs less than any other power transmission medium
Hydraulic systems deliver more power per kilogram than most alternatives
Hydraulic systems never fail, making them the safest option available

hook.text: A tiny seal failure can shut down a 50-ton excavator. Seals are the unsung heroes of fluid power.

buildup.text: O-rings, lip seals, and piston rings prevent fluid from leaking past moving parts. They contain the pressure.

discovery.text: The seal must be soft enough to conform to the surface but tough enough to resist pressure and wear.

twist.text: Heat degrades rubber seals. A hydraulic system running too hot destroys seals, causing leaks that worsen overheating.

climax.text: Modern polyurethane and PTFE seals handle 400 bar and 200 degrees Celsius. Material science keeps fluids contained.

punchline.text: A rubber ring holds back tons of force. Small part, critical job.

quiz.question: What causes a destructive cycle in overheated hydraulic systems?
options: Overheated fluid expands and bursts the hoses from internal pressure
Heat degrades seals, causing leaks that reduce cooling and worsen overheating
High temperature thickens the fluid, blocking flow through narrow passages

hook.text: A hydraulic cylinder converts fluid pressure into a straight push or pull. It's the muscle of heavy machinery.

buildup.text: Oil enters one side of the piston and pushes it outward. The rod extends, applying force to the load.

discovery.text: Force equals pressure times piston area. A 10-centimeter piston at 200 bar pushes with over 15 tons of force.

twist.text: The rod side has less area than the cap side. Retraction is faster but weaker. Extension is slower but stronger.

climax.text: Excavator arms, dump truck beds, and aircraft landing gear all depend on hydraulic cylinders for controlled motion.

punchline.text: Oil in, rod out. That's how machines lift the world.

quiz.question: Why is a hydraulic cylinder stronger during extension than retraction?
options: The pump delivers more pressure during the extension stroke
The cap side has a larger piston area than the rod side, creating more force
The oil flows faster during extension, building more momentum

hook.text: A hydraulic pump doesn't create pressure. It creates flow. Pressure builds only when the flow meets resistance.

buildup.text: Gear pumps trap oil between teeth and the housing. They're simple, cheap, and handle dirty fluid well.

discovery.text: Vane pumps use sliding blades in a slotted rotor. They deliver smoother flow than gear pumps at moderate pressure.

twist.text: Piston pumps handle the highest pressures — over 400 bar. They're complex, expensive, but unmatched in performance.

climax.text: Variable-displacement piston pumps adjust flow on demand. The system uses only the energy it needs.

punchline.text: The pump moves oil. The load decides the pressure.

quiz.question: What type of hydraulic pump handles the highest operating pressures?
options: Gear pumps with hardened steel teeth and tight clearances
Piston pumps that can exceed 400 bar of pressure
Vane pumps with reinforced sliding blades

hook.text: A hydraulic motor is a pump running backward. Oil flows in, the shaft spins out. Fluid power becomes rotation.

buildup.text: Pressurized fluid pushes on gear teeth, vanes, or pistons inside the motor. The imbalance creates torque.

discovery.text: Hydraulic motors deliver high torque at low speed — perfect for driving wheels, winches, and augers.

twist.text: An electric motor the size of a basketball equals a hydraulic motor the size of a fist. Hydraulics win on density.

climax.text: Skid-steer loaders drive each wheel with a separate hydraulic motor. Spin them opposite ways and the machine pivots.

punchline.text: Pump oil in. Get rotation out. Compact, powerful, versatile.

quiz.question: What advantage do hydraulic motors have over electric motors of the same output?
options: They run more efficiently at all speeds and loads
They are much smaller and lighter for the same torque output
They don't require any maintenance or fluid changes

hook.text: An accumulator stores pressurized fluid for when the pump can't keep up. It's a hydraulic battery.

buildup.text: A bladder accumulator has a gas-filled bladder inside a steel shell. Oil enters, compresses the gas, and waits.

discovery.text: When demand spikes, the compressed gas pushes oil out instantly. The system responds without waiting for the pump.

twist.text: Accumulators also absorb pressure spikes. When a valve slams shut, the accumulator cushions the shock wave.

climax.text: Emergency brakes on wind turbines use accumulators. If power fails, stored fluid pressure stops the blades.

punchline.text: Store pressure. Release on demand. The hydraulic safety net.

quiz.question: How does a bladder accumulator store energy?
options: It heats the hydraulic fluid to increase its internal energy
Incoming oil compresses a gas-filled bladder, storing potential energy
A spring inside the shell mechanically stores the pump's energy

hook.text: Particles smaller than a grain of sand can destroy a hydraulic pump. Filters keep the oil clean.

buildup.text: Metal shavings, rubber fragments, and dirt circulate in used oil. They wedge between precision surfaces and score them.

discovery.text: A 10-micron filter catches particles invisible to the naked eye. Most hydraulic failures trace back to contamination.

twist.text: New oil isn't clean enough. It must be filtered before entering the system. Even fresh oil carries contaminants.

climax.text: Changing filters on schedule costs a few dollars. Replacing a destroyed pump costs thousands. Prevention wins.

punchline.text: Clean oil runs forever. Dirty oil destroys everything.

quiz.question: Why must even new hydraulic oil be filtered before use?
options: New oil is too thick and must be filtered to reduce viscosity
Even fresh oil from the container carries invisible contaminants
Filtering adds necessary chemical additives to the oil

hook.text: A hydraulic hose burst sprays oil at 200 bar. It can cut through skin like a knife. Never touch a leaking hose.

buildup.text: Hoses are multi-layered — inner rubber for sealing, braided steel for strength, outer rubber for protection.

discovery.text: Fittings must match the hose size and pressure rating. A mismatched fitting is a leak waiting to happen.

twist.text: Hoses flex and absorb vibration. Rigid steel pipes would crack at every joint on a bouncing excavator.

climax.text: Hoses have a shelf life. UV light and heat degrade rubber over time. Replace them before they fail.

punchline.text: A hose carries power. Respect the pressure inside it.

quiz.question: Why are flexible hoses used instead of rigid pipes on mobile equipment?
options: Flexible hoses cost less than rigid steel piping to install
Hoses flex and absorb vibration that would crack rigid pipes
Hoses provide higher flow rates than equivalent diameter pipes

hook.text: An air compressor squeezes atmospheric air into a tank. That stored pressure powers tools, brakes, and automation.

buildup.text: Reciprocating compressors use pistons. Rotary screw compressors trap air between meshing helical screws.

discovery.text: Compressing air heats it. An intercooler removes that heat between stages so the next stage works more efficiently.

twist.text: Compressors are the biggest energy consumers in most factories. Up to 30% of industrial electricity goes to them.

climax.text: Variable-speed compressors adjust output to demand. They save 30% energy compared to fixed-speed models.

punchline.text: Squeeze air into a tank. You just made a power supply.

quiz.question: Why are air compressors the largest electricity consumers in many factories?
options: They must run continuously regardless of air demand levels
Compressing air requires enormous energy — up to 30% of industrial electricity
They power every machine on the factory floor directly

hook.text: A pneumatic cylinder moves with a quick snap. Compressed air rushes in, the piston flies forward, the part ejects.

buildup.text: Like hydraulic cylinders, pneumatic ones use pressure on a piston. But air compresses, so motion is cushioned.

discovery.text: Pneumatic cylinders are lighter, cheaper, and simpler than hydraulic ones. No oil tank, no return lines needed.

twist.text: Air's compressibility makes precise positioning difficult. The piston bounces and drifts. Exact stops need mechanical limits.

climax.text: Assembly lines, packaging machines, and sorting systems use millions of pneumatic cylinders for fast, repetitive motion.

punchline.text: Fast, cheap, good enough. Air power runs the factory floor.

quiz.question: Why is precise positioning difficult with pneumatic cylinders?
options: Air pressure fluctuates too much for consistent piston movement
Air compresses, causing the piston to bounce and drift past target positions
Pneumatic seals have too much friction to allow fine adjustments

hook.text: Raw compressed air is wet, dirty, and unregulated. An FRL unit cleans it, controls it, and oils it before use.

buildup.text: The filter removes water droplets and particles. Water in air lines causes rust, ice, and valve malfunction.

discovery.text: The regulator drops supply pressure to a consistent working level. Tools need stable pressure to function properly.

twist.text: The lubricator adds a fine oil mist to the air stream. Moving parts inside tools and cylinders need lubrication.

climax.text: Without an FRL unit, pneumatic tools wear out in weeks instead of years. Three simple devices save thousands.

punchline.text: Filter, regulate, lubricate. Three steps to reliable air power.

quiz.question: What does the regulator in an FRL unit do?
options: It removes moisture and particles from the compressed air stream
It reduces and stabilizes supply pressure to a consistent working level
It injects a fine oil mist to lubricate downstream components

hook.text: A suction cup picks up a glass sheet. No clamps, no magnets — just atmospheric pressure pushing from outside.

buildup.text: A vacuum pump removes air from a sealed space. Atmospheric pressure on the outside does the holding work.

discovery.text: At sea level, atmosphere pushes with about one kilogram per square centimeter. A large cup holds surprising weight.

twist.text: You can't pull harder than one atmosphere. Perfect vacuum is the limit. For more force, you need bigger cups.

climax.text: Robots in car factories lift windshields, circuit boards, and body panels with vacuum grippers. Clean and gentle.

punchline.text: Remove the air. Let the atmosphere do the gripping.

quiz.question: What actually holds objects to a vacuum gripper?
options: The vacuum pump creates a magnetic pull on the object's surface
Atmospheric pressure on the outside pushes the object against the cup
Static electricity generated by air removal attracts the object

topics.title: Pneumatic Logic: Air as a Computer

hook.text: Before electronics, factories used air signals to control machines. Pneumatic logic ran entire assembly lines.

buildup.text: Air pressure represents on. No pressure means off. Small valves act as AND, OR, and NOT gates.

discovery.text: Combinations of these air gates created sequences — extend cylinder A, wait, retract, then extend cylinder B.

twist.text: Pneumatic logic has no circuit boards to fry. In explosive environments like paint booths, electric sparks are deadly.

climax.text: Even today, some hazardous environments rely on pneumatic logic. No electricity means no ignition risk.

punchline.text: Air can think — slowly, safely, and spark-free.

quiz.question: Why is pneumatic logic still used in explosive environments?
options: It processes signals faster than electronic controllers
Air-based systems produce no electrical sparks that could cause ignition
Pneumatic components cost less than electronic equivalents

topics.title: Pneumatic Conveying: Moving Materials by Air

hook.text: Grain elevators move tons of wheat through pipes using airflow alone. A fan and a tube replace belts and buckets.

buildup.text: A blower pushes air through a pipe. Material enters the stream and rides along. A separator at the end catches the product.

discovery.text: Dilute-phase systems use fast air to suspend particles. Dense-phase uses pressure pulses to push slugs through the pipe.

twist.text: Enclosed pipes mean no dust, no spills, no contamination. Food and pharma plants choose pneumatic conveying for cleanliness.

climax.text: Cement plants, flour mills, and plastics factories all move bulk materials this way. Air does the heavy lifting.

punchline.text: Blow air through a pipe. The material follows. No belts, no mess.

quiz.question: Why do food and pharmaceutical plants prefer pneumatic conveying?
options: It moves material faster than any belt or bucket system
Enclosed pipes eliminate dust, spillage, and contamination
It uses less energy than mechanical conveyors

hook.text: A directional valve decides where fluid goes. Shift the spool and oil flows to extend. Shift again to retract.

buildup.text: A spool inside the valve body has lands and grooves. Moving the spool connects or blocks different ports.

discovery.text: A 4/3 valve has four ports and three positions — extend, neutral, and retract. One valve controls the whole cylinder.

twist.text: The center position matters. Some center positions lock the cylinder. Others let it float free. Design chooses.

climax.text: Solenoid-operated directional valves respond to electrical signals. A computer now decides which way the fluid flows.

punchline.text: Move the spool. Redirect the river. Control the machine.

quiz.question: What does the center position of a 4/3 directional valve determine?
options: How fast the fluid flows through the valve in either direction
Whether the cylinder locks in place, floats, or slowly drifts when idle
The maximum pressure the valve can handle during operation

topics.title: Pressure Relief Valves: The Safety Limit

hook.text: If a cylinder stalls, the pump keeps pushing oil. Without a relief valve, something explodes.

buildup.text: A spring-loaded poppet blocks the drain port. When pressure exceeds the spring setting, the valve opens and oil dumps to tank.

discovery.text: The relief valve caps system pressure. No component ever sees more force than the valve setting allows.

twist.text: A stuck-open relief valve dumps all flow to tank. The system has full flow but zero pressure. Nothing moves.

climax.text: Every hydraulic system has at least one relief valve. It's the most important safety device in the circuit.

punchline.text: The relief valve exists for the worst case. Without it, the worst case wins.

quiz.question: What happens if a pressure relief valve gets stuck open?
options: System pressure builds dangerously because oil can't escape
All flow dumps to the tank and the system loses pressure — nothing moves
The pump speeds up to compensate for the lost fluid volume

hook.text: A flow control valve restricts how much fluid passes per second. Less flow means the cylinder moves slower.

buildup.text: A needle valve uses a tapered pin to create a variable restriction. Turn the knob to adjust flow precisely.

discovery.text: Meter-in controls flow entering the cylinder. Meter-out controls flow leaving. Meter-out gives smoother control.

twist.text: Temperature changes affect oil viscosity. Thicker oil flows slower through the same valve opening, changing the speed.

climax.text: Pressure-compensated flow controls maintain constant flow regardless of pressure changes. Stable speed in all conditions.

punchline.text: Restrict the flow. Control the speed. Precision in a turn of a knob.

quiz.question: Why does meter-out flow control give smoother cylinder motion than meter-in?
options: It forces oil through the valve at a higher pressure for more consistent flow
It maintains back-pressure on the piston's exhaust side, preventing lunging under load
It heats the oil more, reducing viscosity for easier flow control

hook.text: A check valve lets fluid flow in one direction only. Reverse flow pushes a ball or poppet onto its seat.

buildup.text: Spring pressure keeps the valve closed. Forward flow must exceed the cracking pressure to push it open.

discovery.text: Pilot-operated check valves can be overridden by a pressure signal. This lets you unlock a cylinder when needed.

twist.text: Without check valves, a hydraulic cylinder holding a load would slowly sink as oil leaked back through the circuit.

climax.text: Check valves protect pumps from backflow, hold loads overhead, and isolate circuit branches. Tiny but essential.

punchline.text: One direction only. The simplest rule, enforced by a ball and a spring.

quiz.question: Why are pilot-operated check valves used with hydraulic cylinders?
options: They allow the cylinder to extend faster by bypassing the pump
They lock the cylinder in position but can be overridden when needed to lower the load
They filter contamination from the oil before it enters the cylinder

hook.text: A standard valve is either open or closed. A proportional valve opens any amount you ask — 10%, 47%, 83%.

buildup.text: An electric current moves the spool proportionally. More current means more opening. Flow scales smoothly.

discovery.text: Servo valves add feedback. They measure actual spool position and correct it thousands of times per second.

twist.text: Servo valves cost ten times more than proportional ones. But when a robotic arm needs micron accuracy, nothing else works.

climax.text: Flight simulators use servo hydraulics. The platform moves so precisely that pilots feel real flight forces.

punchline.text: Tell the valve exactly how much. It opens exactly that. Precision on demand.

quiz.question: What makes servo valves more precise than proportional valves?
options: They use stronger magnets to move the spool with more force
They include feedback that measures and corrects spool position continuously
They operate at higher pressures for finer control of flow

hook.text: A joystick sends an electrical signal. A computer processes it. Proportional valves move a 50-ton excavator arm.

buildup.text: Sensors measure pressure, position, and temperature. The controller adjusts valve openings hundreds of times per second.

discovery.text: Closed-loop control means the system constantly corrects itself. Command a position and it holds it against any load.

twist.text: Software can limit forces to protect the machine. An excavator won't tip over because the computer prevents it.

climax.text: Modern hydraulic machines are software-defined. Update the code and the same hardware behaves differently.

punchline.text: Fluid muscle. Digital brain. The best of both worlds.

quiz.question: How do electrohydraulic systems prevent excavator tip-overs?
options: They use heavier counterweights that automatically deploy when needed
Software limits forces and positions to keep the machine within safe boundaries
They lock all cylinders simultaneously when tilt sensors detect danger

hook.text: Press the brake pedal and four wheels stop simultaneously. Hydraulic fluid carries your foot pressure to every caliper.

buildup.text: A master cylinder converts pedal force into fluid pressure. Brake lines carry that pressure to calipers at each wheel.

discovery.text: The calipers squeeze pads against rotors. Friction converts kinetic energy into heat. The car slows down.

twist.text: ABS pumps the brakes 15 times per second during a skid. Hydraulic valves release and reapply pressure faster than any foot.

climax.text: Dual circuits ensure that if one brake line leaks, the other two wheels still stop the car. Redundancy saves lives.

punchline.text: Your foot pushes fluid. Fluid pushes pads. Pads stop tons of steel.

quiz.question: Why do car brake systems use dual hydraulic circuits?
options: To provide stronger braking force on the front wheels than the rear
So that if one circuit leaks, the remaining circuit can still stop the car
To allow the driver to brake the front and rear independently

hook.text: An excavator has no gears in its arm. Every motion — boom, stick, bucket, swing — is pure hydraulic power.

buildup.text: Multiple cylinders work together. The boom lifts, the stick reaches, and the bucket curls — all simultaneously.

discovery.text: The operator controls flow to each cylinder independently. Two joysticks manage six or more motions at once.

twist.text: A large excavator pump moves 500 liters per minute at 350 bar. That's over 200 kilowatts of hydraulic power.

climax.text: No other technology matches hydraulics for this job. Electric actuators can't match the power density.

punchline.text: Oil and cylinders move mountains. That's not a metaphor.

quiz.question: Why do excavators use hydraulics instead of electric actuators?
options: Hydraulic systems are cheaper to maintain than electric ones
Hydraulics provide unmatched power density in the compact space needed
Electric actuators cannot operate outdoors in variable weather

hook.text: A pilot moves the control stick. Hydraulic actuators push the flight surfaces. The plane turns, climbs, or dives.

buildup.text: Aircraft hydraulic systems run at 3,000 PSI — much higher than ground equipment. High pressure means small, light actuators.

discovery.text: Triple-redundant systems ensure that two circuits can fail and the plane still lands safely on the third.

twist.text: Landing gear, brakes, flaps, and cargo doors all run on hydraulics. A single aircraft may have 50 hydraulic actuators.

climax.text: The A380 has eight hydraulic pumps producing 3,500 PSI. Over 100 kilometers of hydraulic tubing runs through the airframe.

punchline.text: Fluid pressure moves wings. Trust in hydraulics at 35,000 feet.

quiz.question: Why do aircraft hydraulic systems operate at much higher pressures than ground equipment?
options: Higher altitude reduces the boiling point of hydraulic fluid
Higher pressure allows smaller, lighter actuators which saves aircraft weight
Aircraft engines produce more power than ground-based pumps

hook.text: An impact wrench blasts lug nuts off in a second. A paint sprayer coats a car panel in minutes. Both run on air.

buildup.text: Air tools are lighter than electric ones — no motor or battery inside. The compressed air is the motor.

discovery.text: Air tools can stall without damage. An electric motor overheats when stalled. An air motor just stops quietly.

twist.text: Air tools waste 90% of the compressor's energy. The compression itself is incredibly inefficient for small tools.

climax.text: Despite the waste, workshops prefer air tools for their lightness, durability, and spark-free operation near fumes.

punchline.text: Inefficient but indestructible. Air tools survive what kills electric ones.

quiz.question: What advantage do pneumatic tools have over electric tools in workshops?
options: They use less energy overall than equivalent electric tools
They are lighter, can stall without damage, and produce no sparks
They run faster and produce more torque than any electric tool

topics.title: Hydraulic Presses: Shaping Metal with Fluid

hook.text: A hydraulic press squeezes 10,000 tons onto a sheet of steel. The metal flows into the die shape like clay.

buildup.text: A large cylinder pushes a ram downward. The die below gives the metal its final shape — a car door, a coin, a pan.

discovery.text: Hydraulic presses apply force evenly across the entire stroke. Mechanical presses peak at one point.

twist.text: The press can hold full force at the bottom of the stroke for as long as needed. Ideal for deep drawing operations.

climax.text: Every car body panel, kitchen sink, and metal can was formed by a hydraulic or mechanical press.

punchline.text: Fluid pressure shapes the objects you touch every day.

quiz.question: What advantage do hydraulic presses have over mechanical ones for deep drawing?
options: They apply force only at the start of the stroke for maximum impact
They can hold full force throughout and at the bottom of the stroke
They operate at higher speeds for faster production cycles

hook.text: Low-rise buildings often use hydraulic elevators. A pump pushes oil into a cylinder beneath the cab, and the cab rises smoothly.

buildup.text: The piston is as tall as the building. Oil flows in and the cab goes up. Release the oil and gravity brings it back down.

discovery.text: Hydraulic elevators are simpler and cheaper than cable types. No overhead machine room, no counterweight, no sheave system.

twist.text: Height is limited — the piston must be buried as deep as the building is tall. Above six floors, cable elevators take over.

climax.text: Roped hydraulic elevators use a pulley to double the travel. The piston needs only half the depth, reaching about ten floors.

punchline.text: Pump oil in. Cab goes up. Let oil out. Cab comes down. Simple.

quiz.question: Why are hydraulic elevators limited to low-rise buildings?
options: Oil pressure drops too much in tall buildings to support the cab weight
The piston must be buried as deep as the building is tall — impractical above six floors
Hydraulic systems are too noisy for taller residential and office buildings
